body:

## Summary

Adds support for wide strings in the `CLI::App` description constructor and `usage()` setter.

* Verified the regression test fails to compile without the new overloads.

title: Fix duplicate option in TOML config output for + option groups
body:
Closes #1449.

A nested option group whose display name starts with `+` (used to flatten its options into the parent's own listing) has its options merged into the parent's option list by `App::get_options()`. But `Config::to_config()`'s subcommand recursion loop still walked into these groups unconditionally, so their options were written out a second time under a separate section.

Beyond the visible duplication in the output, this also breaks reading the config back in: the reported example ends with `2d: too many inputs for a flag`, since the flag's value appears twice in the file and the parser rejects that.

The fix mirrors the exact condition `get_options()` already uses to decide whether a group's options are folded into the parent (`!group.empty() && group.front() == '+'`), and skips the recursive `to_config` call for those groups since their content is already covered by the parent's own pass over its (already-merged) option list.

Added a regression test (`TomlOutputPlusGroupNoDuplication`) reproducing the reported scenario: it checks the duplicate line disappears from the output, and that the round trip through `parse_from_stream` no longer throws.

Ran the config, option-group, subcommand, and app test suites locally; all pass except a single pre-existing failure in `AppTest` (`ensure_utf8_twice`, about argv handling in a spawned helper process) that reproduces identically with or without this change, so it's unrelated to this fix.

title: refactor: return error strings from built-in validators
body:
This seems simpler and removes a bunch of throws.

:robot: _AI text below_ :robot:

Part of #1443.

The built-in validators in `ExtraValidators.hpp` (IsMember, AsNumberWithUnit/AsSizeValue) threw `ValidationError` from inside their `func_` lambdas. `Option::_validate` caught these and flattened them to the `what()` string, so the validator contract (return a non-empty string on failure) already covered them. This change makes the lambdas return the same strings directly. User-visible messages are byte-identical, and the catch in `Option::_validate` stays for user-supplied validators that throw.

The construction-time checks in `AsNumberWithUnit::validate_mapping` still throw, since they report programmer errors and have no string-return channel.

Preparation for `-fno-exceptions` support.

title: build: fix Meson configure error for amalgamated
body:
Meson functions returning project absolute paths (like `meson.current_build_dir()`) should generally be avoided. Here it causes a configure time error with newer Meson.

When building the project with `meson setup build -Dmode=amalgamated`, Meson prints a quite verbose error message exactly spelling out the fix:

```
meson.build:68:26: ERROR: Tried to form an absolute path to a dir in the source tree.
You should not do that but use relative paths instead, for
directories that are part of your project.

To get include path to any directory relative to the current dir do

incdir = include_directories(dirname)

After this incdir will contain both the current source dir as well as the
corresponding build dir. It can then be used in any subdirectory and
Meson will take care of all the busywork to make paths work.

Dirname can even be '.' to mark the current directory. Though you should
remember that the current source and build directories are always
put in the include directories by default so you only need to do
include_directories('.') if you intend to use the result in a
different subdirectory.

Note that this error message can also be triggered by
external dependencies being installed within your source
tree - it's not recommended to do this.
```

This means that `single-include` in source dir will also be considered when looking for includes, but that should be harmless, since that directory contains no code (only an `.in` file).

title: Help not shown for a subcommand if parent subcommand has a positional option
body:
Submitting another issue for #1268, because I can't reopen it. I believe the issue was not solved.
A help for a subcommand subc2 is not shown if subc1 has a positional option and is not provided for the help message.

Below is the minimum reproducible example.
As you can see, .calling `/cli11_help_bug subc1 subc2 --help` provides help on subc1, not subc2.

```shell
$> ./cli11_help_bug subc1 --help
First subcommand


./cli11_help_bug subc1 [OPTIONS] ID [SUBCOMMAND]


POSITIONALS:
  ID INT REQUIRED             Object ID

OPTIONS:
  -h,     --help              Print this help message and exit

SUBCOMMANDS:
  subc2                       Nested subcommand
$> ./cli11_help_bug subc1 subc2 --help
First subcommand


./cli11_help_bug subc1 [OPTIONS] ID [SUBCOMMAND]


POSITIONALS:
  ID INT REQUIRED             Object ID

OPTIONS:
  -h,     --help              Print this help message and exit

SUBCOMMANDS:
  subc2                       Nested subcommand
```

### Reproduction example

```c++
#include <CLI/CLI.hpp>

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    CLI::App app{"CLI11 help bug MRE"};

    auto* subc1 = app.add_subcommand("subc1", "First subcommand");

    int id{};
    subc1->add_option("ID", id, "Object ID")->required();

    auto* subc2 = subc1->add_subcommand("subc2", "Nested subcommand");

    bool flag{false};
    subc2->add_flag("--flag", flag, "Example flag");

    CLI11_PARSE(app, argc, argv);

    return 0;
}
```

Adding positional argument:
```
$ ./cli11_help_bug subc1 1 subc2 --help
Nested subcommand


./cli11_help_bug subc1 subc2 [OPTIONS]


OPTIONS:
  -h,     --help              Print this help message and exit
          --flag              Example flag
```

title: Support colored help output
body: This PR adds support for the colored help output regarding the dicuss in issue: #1285 Functions are added into the `Default Formatter`. When `color_enabled_` is true, ANSI codes are injected into the stream to display various colors. Readme has been updated as well. All tests are passed on my x86 Linux (Arch) machine.

feat: dynamic shell completion, starting with bash
body:
Part of #343. For now only bash is supported, I will work on zsh/fish on later PRs.

Instead of generating a static script that encodes the app's options, the script is a small fixed adaptor: it re-invokes the binary with the line being completed, and the binary replies with candidates and a directive. Rationale in #343. A detailed explanation is included in `book/chapters/completion.md`.

### How to try it out

To see the current state of completion in action (from a bash shell with `bash-completion`):

```bash
cmake --workflow default && cd build
PATH="$PWD/examples:$PATH"
source <(completion --completion bash)
completion <TAB>
# and start playing around with different args
```

To see the wire protocol directly, without a shell in the way:

```console
$ CLI11_COMPLETE=bash CLI11_COMPLETE_INDEX=1 CLI11_COMPLETE_PROTO=1 completion --l
--level       How hard to try
:2
```

### Status

Working end to end for bash:
- Subcommands, including nested ones and aliases
- Option names, with their descriptions
- Values from validators
- `--opt=value`, and values written onto short names and bundles
- Path completion, delegated to the shell
- `--` and `++`
- Positionals, at both multiplicities
- `/flag:value` under `allow_windows_style_options`
- Options and positionals declared in nameless option groups
- Name matching that honours `ignore_case` and `ignore_underscore` the way a parse does

Deliberately not in this PR, happy to follow up:
- zsh, fish and powershell generators
- Per `Option` completion callbacks
- Candidate grouping
- Dot notation (teaching completion that `--sub.opt` takes a value)

Reviewing commit-by-commit will be easier than the squashed diff, as each commit is one capability with its own tests.

title: refactor: add non-throwing name parsing and flag-value paths
body:
:robot: _AI text below_ :robot:

Part of #1443. This removes internal try/catch control flow in three places, in preparation for `-fno-exceptions` support. Thrown types and messages are unchanged.

- `detail::get_names` no longer throws: it reports the applicable `BadNameString` variant through a `name_error` out-parameter, and the `Option` constructor throws the same error. `Split_inl.hpp` no longer needs `Error.hpp`.
- New `Option::try_get_flag_value`, a non-throwing form of `get_flag_value` (which is now a thin throwing wrapper around it). Config output uses it instead of the catch-`ArgumentMismatch` trial-and-error loop.
- `Option::default_val` validates on scratch results and only commits members on success, so it no longer needs catch-based rollback; only the `ConversionError` re-wrap catch remains.

Unit tests cover the new non-throwing paths (success and failure). Verified locally with both the `dev` (precompiled) and `default` (header-only) workflows.

title: refactor: return status from string/encoding detail utilities
body:
:robot: _AI text below_ :robot:

Part of #1443.

Converts the throwing leaf utilities in `detail::` to status-returning functions with an `error_msg` out-parameter, and replaces the try/catch translation blocks at their call sites with direct branches:

- `append_codepoint`, `remove_escaped_characters`, `remove_quotes(vector)`, and `process_quoted_string` return a success flag; a convenience `process_quoted_string` overload without `error_msg` remains for callers that ignore escape errors.
- `narrow_impl`/`widen_impl` gain status-returning overloads; the public `narrow`/`widen` wrappers keep their throwing contract.
- `compute_win32_argv` reports failure through the out-parameter; the throw moves to `App::ensure_utf8`.

Error messages that reach users are byte-identical. New unit tests cover the success and failure paths of the status-returning functions, including the exact error messages. The Windows-only `Argv` change is compile-checked only by CI.

title: refactor: defer config file errors by value instead of exception_ptr
body:
:robot: _AI text below_ :robot:

Part of #1443.

Replace the `std::exception_ptr` in `App::_process()` with a stored copy of the `CLI::FileError` (`std::unique_ptr<CLI::FileError>`), thrown at the same point the exception was rethrown before. This removes the only `std::exception_ptr` use in the library as preparation for `-fno-exceptions` support. The observable behavior (error type, message, exit code, and priority of help/version/requirement errors over config errors) is unchanged.

Also updates the internals chapter of the book and adds a test that `--help` takes priority over a missing required config file, which was not covered before.

title: refactor: handle version flag without exception control flow
body:
:robot: _AI text below_ :robot:

Part of #1443.

The version flag callbacks no longer throw `CallForVersion`. The version string producer is stored on the `App`, the parse path throws when the flag is counted, and `App::version()` calls the stored producer directly instead of catching its own exception. This removes throw-based control flow from the version flag as preparation for `-fno-exceptions` support.

Behavior is unchanged: the same exception and message reach users, and help keeps precedence over version. New tests pin help/version ordering, `--version=false`, and `App::version()` outside a parse. Verified locally with the header-only build in addition to the precompiled dev preset.

title: feat(help): add header() for extended help text after description (#507)
body:
## Summary

Adds `App::header()` / `get_header()` as the complement to the existing `footer()` API, addressing #507.

Extended help text is rendered after the short description and before the usage line in both normal and expanded help output. Subcommand listings in the main help still show only the short description.

## Changes

- `header(std::string)` and `header(std::function<std::string()>)` on `App`, mirroring `footer()`
- `Formatter::make_header()` integrated into `make_help()` and `make_expanded()`
- Header is inheritable from parent apps; cleared for option groups (like footer)
- Tests for header placement, callbacks, and inheritance

## Example

```cpp
auto *fmt = app.add_subcommand("fmt", "Format files in-place.");
fmt->header("If a file is given, it reformats in-place. Otherwise output goes to stdout.");
```

Fixes #507

## Test plan

- [x] `HelpTest`: header appears before Usage in help output
- [x] `HelpTest`: subcommand header not shown in subcommand list
- [x] `CreationTest`: header inherited by subcommands

title: Check to see if anything else can move to pre-compile
body:
🤖 _AI text below_ 🤖 

The review is done — I fanned out four agents over all the declaration headers and spot-checked the key claims. The split is already in good shape (Split, Encoding, Argv, Config.hpp, Formatter.hpp are fully declaration-only), but there is real movable material left, plus a few incidental inconsistencies the review turned up. Here's the synthesis, ranked by value.

## Highest-value moves

**TypeTools.hpp — the two non-template functions in a 1933-line template file.** `detail::to_flag_value` (lines 1081–1126, ~46 lines) and `detail::sum_string_vector` (1878–1929, ~52 lines) are the only non-template bodies there. `sum_string_vector` is only called from `Option_inl.hpp`, so it's already precompiled-side-only in practice; `to_flag_value` also carries two function-local `static const std::string`s whose thread-safe-static guards currently duplicate per TU. The cost is that no `TypeTools_inl.hpp` exists yet, so it needs the full plumbing: the new impl file with `[CLI11:type_tools_inl_hpp:verbatim]` markers, the `#ifndef CLI11_COMPILE` include at the bottom of the header, entries in `src/Precompile.cpp`, the `CLI11_impl_headers` list in CMakeLists.txt, and a slot in `single-include/CLI11.hpp.in` after `{type_tools_hpp}`.

**App.hpp — about two dozen substantive bodies.** The clear ones: `excludes(App*)` (1016–1029, the largest inline body in the header), `excludes(Option*)`, both `needs` overloads, `require_subcommand(int)` / `require_option(int)` (854–863, 883–892), `disabled_by_default` / `enabled_by_default` / `allow_config_extras(bool)` / `callback` (365–372), the `config_to_str` trio, `get_usage` / `get_footer`, the `Option_group` constructor and its `add_option(Option*)` / `add_subcommand(App*)`, and the two `deprecate_option(App…)` free functions (1513–1522). Two caveats:
- `add_flag(std::string, std::function<void(int64_t)>, …)` at 756 sits inside `#ifdef CLI11_CPP14` — moving it means a consumer compiling at a different standard than the lib could see a declared-but-undefined symbol. I'd leave it in the header.
- `get_config_formatter_base()` (1119–1126) branches on `CLI11_USE_STATIC_RTTI` per-TU today; moving it freezes the choice to the lib's setting. Arguably more correct (the current situation is a latent ODR issue for mixed-RTTI builds), but it's a behavior change worth a deliberate call.

**Validators.hpp — finish an inconsistent split.** `description(std::string) const` is already out-of-line but its siblings `name(…) const`, `active(bool) const`, `application_index(int) const` (119–153) are not; same for `operator()(const std::string&)` (93–96) whose non-const twin is already in the impl file. Also `get_description()` and the two non-trivial `Validator` constructors, though note those ctors are called from template ctors in ExtraValidators, so instantiations become cross-TU calls (cold path, fine).

## Moderate value

**Error.hpp** has no `Error_inl.hpp` and is the biggest single chunk: ~150 of its 363 lines are static-factory and constructor bodies (`RequiredError::Option` at 238–260 is 22 lines with six return paths, plus the `ArgumentMismatch`, `ExtrasError`, `BadNameString`, `IncorrectConstruction`, `ConversionError` factories). It would read much better as pure declarations. Two reasons it ranks below the others: it needs the same new-file plumbing as TypeTools, and errors are the one thing *user code* constructs and throws directly — moving the ctors makes those link-time dependencies on the library, which matters most for a Windows shared build (there's no export macro; `CLI11_INLINE` is just `inline`-or-nothing). I'd leave the `CLI11_ERROR_DEF`/`CLI11_ERROR_SIMPLE` macro-generated ctors alone regardless.

**ConfigFwd.hpp / FormatterFwd.hpp** — a handful each: `Config::to_flag` (70–78), `ConfigItem::fullname()` (43–48, which also contains an unreachable `(void)multiline;` after its `return`), the `ConfigINI` constructor, `FormatterBase::get_label` and `long_option_alignment_ratio`, `FormatterLambda::make_help`. Several are virtual, so moving them usefully anchors vtables in the lib — but only fully if the inline empty destructors (`~FormatterBase() {}` at 90) move too, which is an ABI-visible change for anyone mixing header-only and precompiled objects. One systemic caveat: `App.hpp` includes the `*Fwd` headers without their non-fwd siblings, so moving bodies out breaks direct `#include <CLI/App.hpp>` header-only usage (unsupported per the IWYU-private banners, but it works today).

**Option.hpp** is already well split; ~45 lines remain, best being `get_single_name()` (600–611), the protected constructor, `capture_default_str`, `needs(Option*)`, and `clear()`. The `check_sname/lname/fname` trio is on the hot argument-matching path — I'd keep those inline.

## Deliberately leave in the headers

The ~150 one-line getters/setters across App/Option/Config/Formatter/Validators. They're technically movable but there's no readability win, and in precompiled mode you'd trade free inlining for out-of-line calls on accessors that parsing hits in loops. Same for `pre_callback()` (an empty virtual whose move would create a key function and change vtable emission) and the test-only `detail::AppFriend` helpers.

## Incidental findings worth fixing regardless (verified)

1. **Gate mismatch:** `ExtraValidators.hpp:8` tests `CLI11_ENABLE_EXTRA_VALIDATORS != 0` but `ExtraValidators_inl.hpp:12` tests `== 1` — a consumer defining the macro to any value other than 1 can see declarations without definitions in header-only mode.
2. **Inconsistent inline macro:** the two `deprecate_option(App…)` overloads at `App.hpp:1513` and `1519` use plain `inline` while every sibling (`retire_option`, the `Option*` overload) uses `CLI11_INLINE` with an out-of-line body.
3. **Missing `CLI11_MODULE_INLINE`:** `ReadPermissions` / `WritePermissions` / `ExecPermissions` / `NonEmptyFile` (`ExtraValidators.hpp:622–631`) are plain namespace-scope `const` globals — internal linkage, per-TU copies and initializers — unlike every other global validator, which is a module-mode inconsistency.

If you want to act on this, my suggested first PR would be the low-risk, no-new-file set: the App.hpp bodies (minus the two macro-caveat ones), Validators.hpp consistency fixes, Option.hpp's handful, and the three incidental fixes. TypeTools and Error would each be their own follow-up since they need new impl files, and Error deserves a decision on the Windows shared-library linkage question first.

title: Prepare for localization
body:
I'm a bit curious why there are no attempt on preparing the CLI11 lib for [internationalization and localization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internationalization_and_localization) (i18n/l10n)? I'm using this lib in an app that is localized, and it is slightly weird to see strings in English sprinkled in between the localized strings.

Seems like there are a number of patchwork strings, which are difficult to localize. There are also a bit messy separation between logic and messages in some parts of the code, which is a bit cumbersome, but other than that it should be possible.

If the lib is to be prepared for localization, ie internationalized, then it should be set up in such a way that the system can be replaced or simply turned off. Not all want a specific system, although I usually use [GNU gettext](https://www.gnu.org/software/gettext/). It is easy to turn of by setting up a simple define, and it is available on virtually every platform

title: Add an optional extra "long help" message argument to App  (and subcommands)
body:
Right now one can create a subcommand as follows:
```c++
CLI::App &fmt = *app.add_subcommand("fmt", "Format the input files and modifies them in-place.");
fmt.add_option("file", arg_fmt_file, "Source file to format in-place")->required();
fmt.add_option("--spaces", arg_fmt_indent, "Number of spaces to use for indentation", true);
...
```

Which translates to the following help messages:

```
$ lfortran -h
...
Subcommands:
  fmt                    Format the input files and modifies them in-place.

$ lfortran fmt -h
Format the input files and modifies them in-place.
Usage: lfortran fmt [OPTIONS] file

Positionals:
  file TEXT REQUIRED     Source file to format in-place

Options:
  -h,--help              Print this help message and exit
  --spaces INT=4         Number of spaces to use for indentation
  --indent-in-sub        Indent statements in subroutines / functions
  --indent-in-mod        Indent subroutines / functions in modules
  --show                 Show the formatted output, do not modify the original file
  --no-color             Do not "--show" source code in color
```

The current default help message is the "short help", which is displayed in the main app, and it is a good habit to fit on one line to be usable. Then this message is also shown at the top of the subcommand help on one line.

However, in addition to "short help", I would also like to provide a "long help" message, that would show in the subcommand help as follows:
```
$ lfortran fmt -h
Format the input files and modifies them in-place.

Usage: lfortran fmt [OPTIONS] file

If <file> is given, it reformats the files. If -i is specified
together with <file>, the files are edited in-place. Otherwise, the
result is written to the standard output.

Positionals:
  file TEXT REQUIRED     Source file to format in-place

Options:
  -h,--help              Print this help message and exit
  --spaces INT=4         Number of spaces to use for indentation
  --indent-in-sub        Indent statements in subroutines / functions
  --indent-in-mod        Indent subroutines / functions in modules
  --show                 Show the formatted output, do not modify the original file
  --no-color             Do not "--show" source code in color
```

The code to achieve it could be something like:

title: Recursive needs processing
body:
The current way needs relations are checked in void App::_process_requirements() is missleading.
Assume you have an application 'test' with a CLI11 config system configuring following needs relations between some subcommands:

```
app ---> sub1 ---> sub11
     |         |-> sub12
     |-> sub2 ---> sub21
```
A) Current needs processing gives:
```
./test                              -> test requires sub2  // OK for the user
./test sub2                         -> test requires sub1  // OK for the user
./test sub2 sub1                    -> sub2 requires sub21 // Confuses user
./test sub2 sub1 sub21              -> sub1 requires sub12 // Confuses user
./test sub2 sub1 sub21 sub12        -> sub1 requires sub11 // Hm
./test sub2 sub1 sub21 sub12 sub11  -> complete
```

B) Recursive needs processing gives:
```
./test                              -> test requires sub2  // OK
./test sub2                         -> sub2 requires sub21 // More intuitive for user
./test sub2 sub21                   -> test requires sub1  // More intuitive for user
./test sub2 sub21 sub1              -> sub1 requires sub12 // OK
./test sub2 sub21 sub1 sub12        -> sub1 requires sub11 // OK
./test sub2 sub21 sub1 sub12 sub11  -> complete
```

title: Add support for Unicode string in app usage under windows
Rules for positional options
body:
Positional arguments seem to be a topic of interest and figuring out how the matching should be done in relation to unlimited positional arguments and some other modifiers is a bit ad-hoc at the moment.  

**Positional rules**
A positional argument will match the first option not filled searched in order

1. of Definition in the main app
2. By order of definition in any option_groups which are themselves ordered by order of definition.
3. positional arguments fall through to a parent if not otherwise matched.

**if** `validate_positionals` is active,  then the additional consideration is that an argument must pass validation to match.

**if** `positionals_at_end` is active then positional options with the `required` flag will be filled with priority over non-required positionals options if insufficient arguments remain to fill any options beyond the required ones.  

A question for anyone interested is are these rules sufficient or is more fine grained control necessary and if so what might that look like.

title: Ability to modify exception messages
body:
We are using CLI11 for an app. We have done a lot of tinkering with the output. One of the things we ran into during this was the lack of control for the formatting of exceptions.  A lot of my problems are similar to the problems mentioned in issue [167](https://github.com/CLIUtils/CLI11/issues/167)  

Take the following code in app.cpp:

```cpp
    if(min_num > collected) {  // if we have run out of arguments and the minimum was not met
        throw ArgumentMismatch::TypedAtLeast(op->get_name(), min_num, op->get_type_name());
    }
````

```cpp
    CLI11_ERROR_DEF(ParseError, ArgumentMismatch)
    CLI11_ERROR_SIMPLE(ArgumentMismatch)
    ArgumentMismatch(std::string name, int expected, std::size_t received)
        : ArgumentMismatch(expected > 0 ? ("Expected exactly " + std::to_string(expected) + " arguments to " + name +
                                           ", got " + std::to_string(received))
                                        : ("Expected at least " + std::to_string(-expected) + " arguments to " + name +
                                           ", got " + std::to_string(received)),
                           ExitCodes::ArgumentMismatch) {}

    static ArgumentMismatch AtLeast(std::string name, int num, std::size_t received) {
        return ArgumentMismatch(name + ": At least " + std::to_string(num) + " required but received " +
                                std::to_string(received));
    }
  ```

As you can see here, the entire context is essentially lost as everything is combined into a string, making it incredibly difficult to modify this at a later stage. 

So, for me, the solution would be either what is mentioned in the original issue and store information in the exception about the context, or what I think would be even better is to allow the user, like for many other things, to specify a callback for these default build in errors. So, the user gets the ability to build the desired output format.

title: Hooking custom enum serialization framework into CLI11
body:
This is the problem that I have:
* Given an enum serialization framework like [magic_enum](https://github.com/Neargye/magic_enum),
* Make CLI11 use it for all enums that the framework supports,
* Automatically, as in w/o repeating myself for each of the supported types.

And it seems right now this is simply impossible to do.

There is a `lexical_cast` customization point, but I cannot overload it for a constrained set of types because that would result in an ambiguous overload. To be clear, this is what I'm talking about, in user code:
```cpp
template<class T> requires is_supported_by_magic_enum_v<T>
bool lexical_cast(const std::string &s, T &value) {
    // call magic_enum::enum_cast here.
}
```

This produces an ambiguous overload, and the only way around is to provide a `lexical_cast` overload for each of the types. Which is tedious.

Solutions as I see them:


### First
Add another layer in the implementation of `CLI::detail::lexical_cast`:
```cpp
template<class T>
bool lexical_cast(const std::string &s, T &value) {
    return lexical_cast_impl(s, value);
}
// All existing implementations of lexical_cast are renamed to lexical_cast_impl
```

This way, the overload in the first example would work.

However, there is also functionality in CLI that converts enums to strings, so probably I should introduce a customization layer there too? I'd appreciate some pointers on where to look.


### Second
Just add a #define for "don't do enums", the way [nlohmann_json](https://json.nlohmann.me/api/macros/json_disable_enum_serialization/) does it.

Then if it's defined, `lexical_cast` for enums will route through the default streaming implementation, and providing the following overload should solve the issue:
```cpp
template<class T> requires is_supported_by_magic_enum_v<T>
std::istream& operator>>(std::istream &stream, T &value) {
    // call magic_enum::enum_cast here.
    return stream;
}
```

This, however, forces the user to either:
1. Define `operator<<` in the type's namespace so that it's available via ADL, which might not be desirable. After all, `operator<<` is not CLI11's extension point, but an extension point of the C++ standard library.
2. Define `operator<<` in `namespace CLI` or `namespace CLI::detail`, and make sure to pay attention to include order – the headers defining the `operator<<` should go before CLI11 headers. IMO, this is a no-go, users should be free to order their includes the way they want to.


### So

I think it would make sense to implement the first solution above. If this sounds good, I will send in a PR.

Also, I'd be happy to have the second option implemented too, because I want enum parsing from the command line to either route through my custom code, or not compile at all. If this is something that CLI users might find valuable, I'd also be happy to implement it and send in a PR.

title: [Question] How to allow flags in a multiple arguments option (or how to name the remaining() in the help)

CPACK_SOURCE_IGNORE_FILES should be regex- not globs
body:
Disclaimer: I am just trying to interpret the CMake docs and I may have made mistakes. I am still learning about CPack.

[`CPACK_SOURCE_IGNORE_FILES` uses regex- not globs](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/module/CPack.html#variable:CPACK_SOURCE_IGNORE_FILES)

> Pattern of files in the source tree that won't be packaged when building a source package. This is a list of regular expression patterns (that must be properly escaped)

Additionally, [see these notes about `CPACK_VERBATIM_VARIABLES`](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/module/CPack.html#variable:CPACK_VERBATIM_VARIABLES):

> If set to `TRUE`, values of variables prefixed with `CPACK_` will be escaped before being written to the configuration files, so that the cpack program receives them exactly as they were specified. If not, characters like quotes and backslashes can cause parsing errors or alter the value received by the cpack program. Defaults to `FALSE` for backwards compatibility.

Some of the current entries in this repo are written as if they were globs. `/\\\\.DS_Store` seems to be the right idea: the four backslashes become two in the generated configuration file, which becomes one literal backslash. It could possibly be improved as "`/\\\\.DS_Store$`" (trailing `$`).

If you wanted to avoid the whole escaping fiasco altogether, I believe you could use [bracket arguments](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/manual/cmake-language.7.html#bracket-argument) (available starting CMake 3.0) combined with `CPACK_VERBATIM_VARIABLES` (available starting CMake 3.4, which is the minimum supported by this project).

If I'm not accidentally spewing nonsense here, this probably isn't that important given that nobody seems to have noticed it. I don't think source packaging is a very widely used feature of CMake.

* ~~When invoked with such a flag (`--hexplain`) an app should parse its command line and print into stdout a human-readable text explaination of the actuall args used. Its exact appearance is at discretion of CLI parsing library, but it must have the following features:~~
    * ~~first it may clear the echo left by a shell and replace it with a syntax-highlighted version of the command it was got by the app.~~

The explaination can be customized via a hook. If there is no hook set up, the description provided by the tool author for help text is shown.~~

```cpp
// [tag:name:end]
```

The tag is `cli11`. The valid actions are `includes`, `code`, and `verbatim`. Includes are reduced and sorted. A way to allow protected includes might be needed. Name created a variable with that name, or append to an existing one. Code might be stripped of comments (optionally?).

This would be then used with `.make_single_header_rc` (to set the tag to cli11), and with an input file:

```cpp
// Header (could be from a verbatim)
{preinc}
#if defined(CLI11_COMPILE) || CLI11_COMPILE == 1
{inc}
#endif

namespace CLI {

{optional_fwd}
...

#if defined(CLI11_COMPILE) || CLI11_COMPILE == 1
{optional_inl}
#endif 
...
}  // namespace CLI
```

This is read in and uses Python's format function, with dictionary of variables expanded. Something like this (pseudocode):

```python
c = Combine()
for file in "*_fwd.hpp", "*.inl":
    c += Combine(file)

with open("conf.txt") as f:
    txt = f.read()
single_header = txt.format(**c.dict)
```

The version, etc. could be added as it is now.

See #338.

title: Include order for custom converters
body:
I was trying the support for custom converters described in https://cliutils.gitlab.io/CLI11Tutorial/chapters/advanced-topics.html#custom-converters

I was curious about the constraint to set up the custom `istringstream& operator <<` overload before including CLI11.

Could you provide any pointers as to what's the concrete C++ limitation that doesn't allow us to be more flexible in this sense?

In my experience constraining the ordering of includes is quite tricky and a source of headaches down the road. I guess you may have a very good reason why this cannot be avoided :)

title: Add a move constructor (may not work)
Accumulation of errors for a better message
body:
Hi, 
At parsing step, is it possible, to accumulate the errors, (such as missing required argument or conversion errors, and so on) in order to display all of them at the end at the same time ? For example, returning a big "CLI::ParsingError(error_string)" at the end with an error per line.
In fact, behind the fact that it would be much much easier for the user to have all errors at once, I would like to have the parsing results (I mean, having the option variables filled, at least those given correctly in the command line).
Is it easy to do something like that ?
Thank you.

title: Passing error information though
body:
Hi,
     I wanted to adapt the output from CLI11 to match my local standard, which is Unix style. 
So instead of:

  _The following arguments were not expected: foo bar_

I want:

  _MyProgram: error: unexpected arguments "foo", "bar"_

and instead of:

   _The value Foo is not an allowed value for -Bar_

I want:

  _MyProgram: invalid usage, "Foo" is not an allowed value for option "--Bar"_

I thought no problem I can simply catch the exceptions and translate them.
This is not possible as the exception classes such as "ConversionError" construct the message but do not preserve the parameters needed:

    ConversionError(std::string member, std::string name)
        : ConversionError("The value " + member + " is not an allowed value for " + name) {}

It would be a simple change to make "member" and "name" member variables of the exception class for this and the other errors.
Would a pull request making this change be accepted (assuming I can find the time)?

Regards,

Bruce.
